assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reframed cross-country income differences as a question of how inputs are allocated across firms. This gave a measurable, quantitative account of why some economies stay poor, and it opened a large empirical literature in growth, development and macro. It speaks to long-run divergence, which is a central question for the field.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow's 2009 paper on misallocation in China and India is the anchor. Restuccia (with Rogerson) supplied the closely related theoretical and quantitative framework. The three-name set is coherent. Rogerson is a plausible omission in the credited names, but I am confined to the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of replication, extension and policy use. The core idea has been widely absorbed, so the timing is mature.
uncertainties: Measured misallocation can partly reflect measurement error or unobserved heterogeneity in firm-level data, and the size of the aggregate effects is debated.
Some of the credit may belong to Rogerson, who is not in the credited names.
Recent growth-related prizes could affect how the Committee weighs the topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Used population-scale administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation. This changed what is known empirically about opportunity and shaped policy debate. It is also a data-and-measurement advance in the archival, new-sources spirit I value.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is clearly central, and Hendren and Friedman are repeated co-authors on the main mobility and neighbourhood-effects papers. Katz is also credited, but a three-name limit is more consistent with the core contribution.
assessment.maturity: The major papers date from roughly 2014 to 2022, and follow-up work continues. Policy and academic uptake is large, though the full body of work is still maturing.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is more measurement and empirical craft than a conceptual advance.
Causal interpretation of place effects is still being refined.
Chetty's work spans several candidate topics, which could blur attribution across ballots.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed with linked micro data that household credit expansions drive housing booms and are followed by deeper, longer downturns. The work shifted macro-finance and policy thinking after the 2008 crisis. It combines careful new data with identification.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear joint originators, in the House of Debt programme and the underlying papers. Campbell's mortgage and household finance work is related but distinct, so I would not include him on this topic.
assessment.maturity: More than a decade of evidence and replication since the crisis. Recent prizes in banking and crises have already honoured an adjacent area, so the question is whether this topic is distinct enough.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Debate over how far the credit-supply and household-demand channels explain the downturn.
Campbell's role is separate and arguably not part of this discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technological change and the China-shock studies changed how economists and policymakers understand labour-market adjustment to technology and trade. They show that adjustment is persistent and geographically concentrated. This resonates with current debates on technological change and the people it displaces.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central across both strands. Dorn and Hanson are co-authors on the China-shock work, and the task framework also draws on Autor, Katz and Levy, and on Acemoglu. The credit to Katz is substantial but I would restrict the set to the trade-shock core.
assessment.maturity: Over twenty years of work on tasks and about a decade on trade shocks, with high replication and extension.
uncertainties: Task-model credit overlaps with a recently recognised laureate and with Katz and Levy.
Some China-shock results are contested on identification and on the size of long-run effects.
The three-name limit forces the exclusion of Katz.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed trade theory and empirics: only productive firms export, trade reallocates activity across firms, and gains come through selection as well as through classic channels. It reshaped the field and became a workhorse for measuring the gains from trade.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 paper is the anchor. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple link it to the export-versus-FDI choice, and Redding contributed to the quantitative and spatial extensions. Helpman also appears under another trade-politics ballot, so some of his credit could be split.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of work, with deep confirmation in firm-level data.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the new trade theory prize (Krugman) and with the quantitative trade models ballot.
Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have claims on the same ground, but I am limited to the credited names.
Whether Redding's quantitative-spatial contributions should be included.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal approach to the open economy and the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles provide the standard framework for current-account dynamics, exchange rates and international monetary policy. It is an influential synthesis, and Obstfeld and Rogoff's textbook and papers are widely used.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the natural pair, particularly through the Redux model and the puzzles paper. Other contributors, such as Lane, Gopinath and Engel, are not credited, and this is partly a synthesis of work by many hands.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use, so very mature. Nothing new is needed to confirm its importance.
uncertainties: How much of the contribution is original discovery versus synthesis.
Rogoff is credited on another ballot, so the credit could be split.
The disconnect puzzles remain open, which makes them more a research agenda than a resolved finding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established the modern empirical and theoretical study of how political institutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. The work links economics, politics and history, which I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini built the constitutional political economics programme, and Besley and Persson built the state-capacity work. The trio is coherent. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson already received the 2024 prize on institutions, so the incremental claim here needs care.
assessment.maturity: Long-established, with decades of work and wide empirical testing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity.
Possible concerns about the Committee's ties to Stockholm-based economists, which are disclosed but not adjudicated here.
Whether the constitutional and state-capacity strands count as one discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Constructed long-run top-income and wealth series from tax records and showed the historical evolution of inequality. This is a major data-construction achievement that reopened the study of inequality, and it is close to the historical national accounts tradition. The Committee would also need to weigh its policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the originators of the top-incomes series. Zucman's offshore-wealth work builds on this and is credited separately, but I think two names capture the core discovery.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of series construction and replication, though some interpretations of the wealth-concentration results remain debated.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over how wealth and top-income shares are measured and which taxes are included.
Saez appears on other ballots, so credit could be split.
The theoretical claim about r versus g is more contested than the data construction.
